extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters / patent attorneys / practitioners preparing patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting the description, drawings and abstract of a patent application, and for preparing claims and related material so the application supports broad enforceable claims across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The description of a patent application shall, where this is not self-evident, indicate the way in which the invention is capable of exploitation (industrial applicability). Claims may need to be revised to satisfy industrial applicability requirements in some jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claimed invention (e.g., a device for dispensing fashion advice) might be found to lack industrial applicability, recast claims to a practical, industrially-applicable framing (e.g., device for maintaining inventory levels). Check jurisdictional requirements (see Module II, section 2.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts interpret claims and the description; claim interpretation is typically the most critical factor in determining infringement or validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims and description so their meaning is clear to a person skilled in the art; anticipate that only a few terms may determine scope. Prepare to support claim term meanings in the specification and prosecution history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor ordinary meaning for claim terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts (particularly in the U.S.) begin by giving terms in the claims their ordinary meaning to a person skilled in the art; only then do they consult the description, prosecution history, dictionaries, treatises or expert testimony if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inventing unusual meanings for common terms unless you explicitly define them in the description. Be cautious when relying on external dictionaries; instead, aim for a self-contained application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define new or ambiguous terms in the description
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent application creates a new term, where several meanings are possible and only one is meant, or where a term may be ambiguous, define it in the description section so the application is self-contained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the description as a glossary of special claim terminology. Tie definitions to embodiments and avoid leaving meaning to external sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft claims as though no doctrine of equivalents exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the doctrine of equivalents is unpredictable and varies by jurisdiction, draft claims to give terms their ordinary and customary meaning to a person skilled in the art rather than relying on equivalents for protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek literal coverage of key variants (e.g., use broader terms like 'metal fastener' rather than relying on a court to equate 'nail' with 'screw'). Know the doctrine's reach in each jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prosecution history estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications during prosecution can foreclose application of the doctrine of equivalents in some jurisdictions (prosecution history estoppel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful in office-action responses not to make admissions that restrict claim scope (e.g., asserting 'only' nails are used) if you may later need to argue equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft the broadest main claim(s) early
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafting first the broadest main claim(s) reciting the inventive features is an efficient way of formulating the essential inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use broad independent claims to capture the inventive concept, then draft dependent claims and the description to support and enable them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft description to support claims (order and iteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: After drafting claims, draft the title, technical field, background art and summary (or later as appropriate), then draft brief description of figures, detailed description of embodiments and drawings as a group; revisit and revise claims after drafting the description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iteratively check that claim terms are disclosed and supported in the description and drawings; remove extraneous claim elements that could limit scope; ensure consistency of terms and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title should be broad yet concise
rubrics_metrics.description: The title should describe the subject matter broadly yet concisely; avoid being overly narrow so as not to unduly limit implied scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer broad published-friendly titles (e.g., 'SEMICONDUCTOR DEVICE AND METHOD FOR FABRICATING THEREOF'). In some jurisdictions, avoid headings containing the word 'invention' to prevent narrowing (use 'title' instead of 'title of invention').

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical field brevity and non-inventive statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The technical field section should be a short paragraph (two or three sentences) stating the general technical field without identifying the claimed invention itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate the general classification and expected expertise of the reader (person skilled in the art), but do not state inventive features in this section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background art: set context, identify problem, avoid solution
rubrics_metrics.description: The background art should briefly set out the state of the art and identify the problem the invention addresses; it should disclose only the problem and not the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include only the closest, publicly-available prior art known to the inventor; avoid long historical narratives and avoid modifiers like 'well-known' or 'common'. Beware of inadvertently admitting applicant-admitted prior art (which can be harmful in some jurisdictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution on citing prior art in background
rubrics_metrics.description: Only include prior art that was published and directly relevant; in some jurisdictions listing known prior art references is required, while in others it may be unhelpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-check that inventor-cited prior art is actually prior art under patent law. Place lists of references in the description according to local application format (e.g., CAF).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'objects of the invention' and absolute effect statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'objects of the invention' paragraphs and absolute statements about advantageous effects (e.g., 'noise can be fully eliminated'), as these can narrow the invention or invite objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such statements are required, keep them limited to the problem and use relative expressions ('noise can be reduced' or 'lower noise can be achieved').

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of invention: outline full scope and tie to claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The summary should outline what has been invented in its full scope and explain how the inventor has overcome the background problem; it should, effectively, summarize the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider turning each independent claim into a paragraph in the summary to ensure claim language appears in the description. Include advantageous effects only where they correspond to features of the broadest claims and avoid a broad 'meta' summary that goes beyond the claims and creates risks of implied but undeclared subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brief description of drawings: state figures, type and perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: The brief description of drawings should state what each drawing figure represents, the drawing type (photograph, line drawing, flowchart, etc.), and any visual perspective, and explain how drawings relate to embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a statement that drawings are illustrative of embodiments (where jurisdictional practice suggests) to avoid narrowing claims to only illustrated examples. Provide a short caption per figure (e.g., 'Figure 1 is a diagrammatic representation...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of embodiments must enable and support claim amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: The description of embodiments must (i) reflect inventor-provided disclosure, (ii) provide sufficient information to enable a person skilled in the art to reproduce the invention, and (iii) provide sufficient depth so claims can be narrowed later to avoid prior art cited by an examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include enough detail and alternatives at filing because substantive amendments adding new technical disclosure are generally not permitted after filing. Ensure embodiments are tied to drawings and use reference numerals appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie abstract claim terms to concrete embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: If claims use highly abstract terms, use the description of embodiments to tie those terms to specific examples so the meaning is clear and the term can be construed broadly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., state 'One example of warning device 102 is an automobile horn; other warning devices may be used' and list alternatives (siren, buzzer) to support broader interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance disclosure: err on inclusion to avoid insufficient support
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent drafters should balance the risks of too-bare disclosure versus disclosing too much unclaimed subject matter; generally err on the side of inclusion to preserve options for narrowing claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insufficient description at filing prevents later narrowing to overcome novelty or inventive-step objections. However, be aware excessive unclaimed disclosure may lead to dedication to the public of those aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dedicating unclaimed subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Unclaimed subject matter disclosed in the specification is considered dedicated to the public and cannot later be conferred patent rights unless claimed in an appropriate subsequent filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims before the description or ensure the description is tailored to support intended claims. Use divisional or continuation filings if unity issues reveal unclaimed inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid phrasing that artificially narrows scope ('the invention is ...')
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid saying 'the invention is X'; instead say 'an embodiment of the invention is X' or 'an exemplification of the apparatus/method', to preserve broader interpretation of claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using 'the invention is' risks limiting the claims to the stated characterization and can hinder broad claim interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plain language and avoid jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Use simple technical language rather than jargon or special complex terminology to make it easier for competitors, examiners, or judges to understand terms and reduce risk of unintended meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plain language also eases translation for filing in other jurisdictions. Compile lists of absolute words to search-and-replace (e.g., 'always', 'never').

rubrics_metrics.name: Known features may be omitted if well-known in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent drafter does not need to include well-known material necessary to make or use a product unless the invention modifies that method or feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit well-known steps or parameters that add bulk without technical disclosure (e.g., routine curing procedures) unless they are relevant to the inventive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making context or examples inadvertently limiting
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing components and operation or illustrative drawings, condition discussions to prevent the context or examples from becoming limiting parts of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state that drawings/embodiments are illustrative and include multiple alternatives to support broader claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check jurisdictional presentation and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The headings, order and acceptable content of description sections vary across jurisdictions (e.g., PCT headings, U.S. heading preferences); drafting must follow the presentation customary to each filing jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate precise requirements and customary practice applicable to each jurisdiction; adapt section headings (e.g., use 'summary' instead of 'summary of invention' where helpful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional diligence: consult client and avoid post-filing fixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult the client on every substantive matter and avoid relying on post-filing fixes; substantive technical disclosure cannot usually be added after filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If critical disclosure is missing, consider filing a new application only if not barred by inventor activities or the original filing date. Avoid assumptions about inventor knowledge or intended scope.
